title: Testing push and pull designs
keyIdea: A design is a plan to make something do a job, like a ramp or a push that stops a ball on a mat. To find out if it works, test it and look at what happened. A push changes how fast a ball goes: too gentle and it stops short, too hard and it rolls past, so the hardest push is not always best. To make a ball turn, something has to push it a new way, like a wall or a block in its path; pushing harder only makes it go faster in a straight line. One try can be lucky, so test it several times and record each result as a tick or a cross. Count the ticks to judge the design. If it fails, keep the goal where it is, change one thing in the design and test again.
familyTip: Roll a ball along the floor towards a cushion or a cup lying on its side. Try a gentle push, a medium push and a hard push, and draw a tick or a cross for each one. Then put a book on its side in the ball's path and see if you can make the ball turn into a box.

visual.caption: What should we change? Drag each card into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: Needs a wall to turn it

lab.caption: Flagship lab: try three pushes, test one push five times, drag a wall to turn a ball into a goal, read two ramps' results, and fix failed tests.

kid: We want a ball to stop on a mat. That is the job. Our plan is a design. Is it a good one? Test it and see! A gentle push stops short. A hard push rolls right past. A medium push stops on the mat.
One try can be lucky. So test it again and again. Draw a tick when it works and a cross when it does not. Then count. 4 ticks out of 5 means it works most of the time.
A push makes a ball go faster. But a push in a straight line keeps it going straight. To make it turn, put a wall in its way. The wall pushes it a new way.
If a test goes wrong, do not move the goal. Change the design. Give it a bigger push, a smaller push, or move the wall. Then test it again.
adult: Ages 5 to 6. NGSS K-PS2-2 asks children to analyse data to decide if a design solution works as intended to change the speed or direction of an object with a push or a pull. Examples are a ramp that speeds up a ball and a structure that makes a marble turn. Key words: design, test, push, pull, speed, direction, result, works.

The data here is simple: where the ball stopped, and a tick or a cross for each try. Counting ticks across several tries is the analysis. This links to K-2 engineering (test and compare designs) and to the National Curriculum in England, Years 1 and 2: 'gathering and recording data to help in answering questions'.

Common mistakes: thinking the hardest push is always best; deciding a design works or fails after one try; expecting a harder push to make a ball turn, when only a push from a new direction, such as a wall, changes its direction; moving the goal instead of changing the design; and judging a design by its last try instead of counting all the results.

In the lab, children try three pushes and record each result. They test one push five times and judge it from the tally. They drag a wall to turn a ball into a goal. They read results for two ramps and fix three tests that went wrong.

practice.prompt: Testing push and pull designs: a gentle push stops the ball before the mat. What should you try next?
practice.hint: The ball did not go far enough. Does it need more push or less?
practice.explain: The ball stopped short, so it needs a bigger push. Moving the mat would change the goal, not the design.

practice.prompt: Ava tests her ramp 5 times. The ball lands in the cup {n} times. How many times did it miss?
practice.hint: Take the times it worked away from the 5 tries.
practice.explain: 5 tries take away {n} that worked leaves {=5-n} misses. Counting both tells you how well the design works.

practice.prompt: Ramp A works {a} times. Ramp B works {b} times. How many more times did Ramp B work?
practice.hint: Find the difference: take Ramp A's ticks away from Ramp B's.
practice.explain: {b} take away {a} is {=b-a}. Ramp B worked more times, so it is the better design.

practice.prompt: A ball rolls straight, but the goal is round a corner. How can you make the ball turn?
choices: Put a wall in its way
practice.hint: A push in a straight line keeps it going straight. What could push it a new way?
practice.explain: A wall in the ball's path pushes it a new way, so it turns. A harder push only makes it go faster.

practice.prompt: Leo's car stops on the line on its very first test. What should he do now?
choices: Test it a few more times
Stop testing and move the line
practice.hint: Could one try be lucky? What if the floor is bumpy next time?
practice.explain: One try can be lucky. Testing a few more times shows if the design works most of the time.

pool.prompt: A hard push sends the ball right past the mat. What does that tell you?
choices: The hardest push is always best
The mat is in the wrong place
pool.hint: Did the ball stop on the mat, or go past it?
pool.explain: The ball went past, so the push was too hard. A medium push is the one that stops it on the mat.

pool.prompt: Ramp A: tick, cross, cross, cross, tick. Ramp B: tick, tick, cross, tick, tick. Which works better?
pool.hint: Count the ticks for each ramp.
pool.explain: Ramp B has 4 ticks and Ramp A has only 2, so Ramp B works better.

pool.prompt: Ramp A worked on its last try, but only 2 times out of 5. Ramp B worked 4 times. Which is the better design?
choices: Ramp B, it worked more times
Ramp A, the last try counts most
pool.hint: Every try counts, not just the last one.
pool.explain: Ramp B worked 4 times and Ramp A only 2. Count all the tries to judge a design.

pool.prompt: The ball rolls past the goal. Mia moves the goal further away. Is that a fair fix?
choices: No, she should change the push
Yes, the ball gets there now
pool.hint: Is she changing the design, or the job?
pool.explain: Moving the goal changes the job. A fair fix keeps the goal and changes the design, like a smaller push.

pool.prompt: Which of these makes a rolling ball change direction?
choices: Bumping into a wall at a slant
pool.hint: Pushes from behind keep it going the same way. What pushes it a new way?
pool.explain: A slanted wall pushes the ball a new way, so it turns. Pushes from behind only change its speed.

pool.prompt: Sam tests his launcher {n} times. It misses 1 time. How many times did it work?
pool.hint: Take the 1 miss away from all the tries.
pool.explain: {n} tries take away 1 miss is {=n-1} times it worked. That is most of the time.

pool.prompt: Zoe draws {a} ticks and {b} crosses on her results chart. How many tests did she do?
pool.hint: Each test gets one tick or one cross. Add them up.
pool.explain: {a} ticks and {b} crosses make {=a+b} tests in all.

pool.prompt: Why do we test a design more than once?
choices: One try can be lucky or unlucky
pool.hint: Think about the bumpy floor that made one try stop short.
pool.explain: One try can be lucky or unlucky. Testing several times shows if the design works most of the time.

pool.prompt: A ball stops before the mat on every try. Which change should you test?
choices: Add a wall to turn it
pool.hint: It is going straight, but not far enough.
pool.explain: It goes the right way but not far enough, so it needs a bigger push. Then test it again.
